headline: Motorola teases wide foldable phone to challenge Samsung and Apple
summary: The company shared a silhouette of a wide foldable, hinting at a new competitor in the market for larger foldable devices, similar to Apple's iPhone Duo and Samsung's Z Fold 8.
details: Motorola has officially teased a new wide foldable phone on its social media channels. The brief glimpse shows a silhouette of a device that appears similar in form factor to Apple's rumored iPhone Duo and Samsung's Z Fold 8.

This move suggests Motorola is entering the growing market for larger, tablet-style foldables, a segment that has seen renewed interest despite previous attempts failing to gain widespread traction. Apple's anticipated wider design for its iPhone Duo is seen as a catalyst for other brands to follow suit.

Samsung has already adopted a dual-strategy in the US, offering both wide and tall foldable options. The Z Fold 8, a wider model, is reportedly more popular and cheaper than its taller counterpart, the Z Fold 8 Ultra.

While Motorola has experience with flip-style foldables, its entry into the tablet-foldable market was relatively late, with a previous model announced in January 2026 and released in May 2026. This significant delay between announcement and retail availability could be a challenge for its new wide foldable.

The teaser clip, appearing at the five-second mark, includes the slogan "Just wait for our next move." Although hardware details are scarce, the device's appearance seems consistent with other wide foldables currently available.

A common challenge for foldable phones across brands, including Apple's iPhone Duo, remains camera performance. Many models, including Apple's, feature dual-camera setups that often lack the dedicated telephoto lenses found in their premium non-foldable counterparts.

headline_marked: [[San Francisco orders Meta to stop AI child abuse ads]] after 350+ ads ran on platforms
headline: San Francisco orders Meta to stop AI child abuse ads after 350+ ads ran on platforms
summary: San Francisco's city attorney has issued a cease-and-desist to Meta, demanding it stop "allowing" over 350 paid advertisements featuring AI-generated child sexual abuse content that reached over 29,000 accounts.
details: San Francisco's city attorney has issued a cease-and-desist letter to Meta, demanding the company stop "allowing" paid advertisements that include AI-generated child sexual abuse content. This follows a WIRED report revealing over 350 such ads ran on Meta's platforms in recent months, reaching more than 29,000 accounts.

These ads transformed still images of minors, some confirmed as real individuals, into short video clips depicting sexual acts. When clicked, the ads directed users to download AI apps capable of digitally undressing people or creating other nonconsensual intimate imagery.

Discovered by researchers at the Tech Transparency Project (TTP), some identical ads were uploaded multiple times, targeting accounts in the EU, US, Australia, and India. Notably, over 250 of the total ads ran on Meta’s platforms after WIRED’s initial report in August.

San Francisco City Attorney David Chiu stated Meta "failed to address a known issue" and profited from these "deeply disturbing" ads, which he says cause harm to real children. He criticized Meta's "woefully inadequate" efforts despite claims of zero tolerance for child exploitation.

Meta responded by claiming the ads were "outside the city attorney's jurisdiction" as there was "no indication" they were displayed in San Francisco. However, the City Attorney's Office argues that because San Francisco consumers can access the unlawful ads online, the matter is within their purview.

Meta previously told WIRED that many of the identified ads had already been removed before being reported, and all have now been removed for violating policies. The company also stated most ads had "fewer than 200 impressions" and the total ad spend for the 300-plus ads was "under $5,000."

The letter demands Meta stop the ads, explain how they bypassed moderation, detail its escalation and reporting to the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children (NCMEC), and outline its approach to advertisers and repeat offenders. It suggests "broader systemic problems" with Meta's ad detection systems.
